newsitem.title: MOROCCO: FEATURE-From Morocco's villas to shacks, family ties run deep.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-From Morocco's villas to shacks, family ties run deep.

text.p: From the shacks that form the "bidonvilles" or slums around Casablanca to the villas that grace the capital Rabat, a common power runs through each Moroccan's daily life.
It is the sense of family, whose secrets, ties, and way of life have come under the microscope, showing its strength and impact.
All-pervasive family councils, constant meetings, decide who a girl will marry, where newlyweds will live and when the children will start working.
To Western eyes the concept may seem strange, but many women in conservative Arab countries like Morocco see family involvement as beneficial.

"There is so much prejudice against divorced women that it is better for the family to choose the husband to make sure he is the right man," said 45-year-old Nadia, a divorced woman who chose her own partner.
"I think that if the husband knows the family, he will be careful not to ill-treat his wife."
But another, who asked not to be named, said: "There are many cases where too much family involvement has wrecked marriages."

There is not that much difference in attitude among those living in the modern cities or dwelling in the countryside, from snow-topped Atlas Mountains, across desert to the Atlantic coast, despite the gulf in many other areas.
FAMILIES CHOOSE MARRIAGE PARTNERS
Few Moroccan girls can choose the man they will marry.
"The family 'fingerprint' is still very clear in the choice of partners for the women," says a national official inquiry, recently released, into Moroccan family life.
Only 16.1 percent of women, who outnumber men by nearly 650,000 in the (1995) population of 26 million, made a "strictly personal" choice of their partner.
In the countryside the figure was half that.
"Overall, in 80.2 percent of first unions, family members intervened in the choice of the partner," says the report.
Some women see economic interest at work.

"If both families are wealthy, a marriage is arranged to ensure their fortune will not be undermined, otherwise it's a source of income in poorer families when they combine," said one single woman, Meryem, 32, an economics graduate.
The report backs the point, observing that most newlyweds spend the first years of married life in the home of in-laws.
Mostly, in town and country, it is mother and father who decide for the girl, but other relatives can also have a say.
How well this works is relative. "For 70.3 percent of women, the first marriage lasts forever," say the officials who carried out the survey.

But nearly 30 percent of first marriages do end in one partner being alone. Just over half those splits result from divorce after an average 4.5 years together. The others are caused by death of a partner, often cited by women instead of saying they were divorced.
GIRLS VIEWED AS BURDENS

Nadia, a 37-year-old teacher who withstood pressure to marry, had a different viewpoint on family involvement: "A girl is considered a burden from the start; the sooner the family gets rid of her, the better."

A women's action group, l'Union de l'Action Feminine, says divorce in cities is worse. They cite Casablanca, the country's financial centre and home to more than four million people, where it says more than half of first marriages fail.
While the family group is changing to a more nuclear one, the head of the family is a man in nearly 85 percent of homes.
More than one in five meet their father at least once a week, and 7.2 percent each day. Many also meet their brothers or sisters each day.

Schooling too speaks volumes about family attitudes. Nearly 80 percent of household heads see education as something mainly to increase a girl's knowledge. For sons it is somewhat different. Over 55 percent of the same family heads saw it as a way to help sons find a job.
The report's snapshot of family life shows one reason why girls are seen as useful for starting work for the family earlier in the country than in towns.
Life lacks conveniences and is harder.

Only 15 percent of country families have a "cooker", fewer than one in five a bathroom, compared to 40.1 percent in towns. A toilet graces most city homes (91.8 percent) while in the country under 36 percent have this luxury.

And despite progress in providing drinking water, with 86 percent of urban homes on the network, fewer than one in 10 homes in the country are linked. And just over one in 10 homes there had electricity.
